newsitem.title: HUNGARY: OTP pays 12 pct div, sees rising profits.
newsitem.headline: OTP pays 12 pct div, sees rising profits.

text.p: Hungary's OTP Bank plans a 35.4 percent increase in its after-tax profits to 13.5 billion forints in 1997, continued cost-cutting, a moderate rise in assets, and the development of services, Chairman and CEO Sandor Csanyi told the shareholders on Tuesday.

"The main target this year is the improvement of profitability," Csanyi told the bank's annual general meeting, adding that OTP plans to boost its earnings per share to 478.6 forints in 1997 from 355.2 forints in 1996.

Previously, the shareholders voted to pay on the 1996 earnings a dividend of 12 percent, or 120 forints, compared with a dividend payment on the 1995 earnings of 10 percent on its ordinary shares and 12 percent on preference shares.
Each share has a face value of 1,000 forints.

OTP posted an after-tax profit of 9.94 billion forints in 1996, on assets of 1,256.1 billion forints, compared with an after-tax profit of 6.97 billion forints on assets of 1,027.78 billion forints in 1995.

Csanyi said OTP, which is Hungary's largest commercial bank and has a dominance over banking for retail customers and the local municipalities, will have to continue in 1997 a hard fight with competitors, being strengthened by increasing foreign investment, for retaining its market share.
OTP's balance sheet total accounted for 28 percent of the assets of all Hungarian banks in 1996.
"OTP practically kept its market share in the Hungarian banking sector in 1996," Csanyi said. "We lost one percent last year."
OTP's market share in retail banking was 57 percent at the end of last year, and Csanyi said that its large network and developing services should enable the the bank to keep this market share.
OTP will concentrate on the improvement of the services linked to products it has already sold and retaining good customers, rather than on expanding the number of products sold, Csanyi added.

He said OTP's market share in lending to local municipalities was 71 percent in 1996, down from 77 percent in 1995, while on the deposit side it lost one percent last year, with its market share accounting for 90 percent in 1996.
OTP's market share in corporate deposits was 14 percent in 1996, down from 15 percent in 1995, while it remained flat at 11 percent in corporate lending.
Csanyi said OTP planned a 7.2 percent rise to in non-interest expenditures for 1997, compared with its 17 to 19 percent forecast for average inflation.
The cost-cutting programme will include a 10 percent reduction in the number of employees and the closing of unprofitable branches, he added.
